title: Weaning piglets from the sow
subtitle: Timing, method, and managing the sow and litter through separation.
excerpt: Piglets in a small holding are typically weaned at six to eight weeks of age. Weaning too early increases stress, digestive disease, and post-weaning growth checks. Too late reduces the sow's recovery time and the number of litters she can raise in a year. Here is the standard approach to weaning, what to feed newly weaned piglets, and how to manage the sow afterwards.
sourceNotes: BPEX, pig management guide (2015). RSPCA, pig welfare requirements. NADIS, weaning piglets guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: A high-specification, easily digestible dry feed offered to piglets from around two weeks of age through a small opening the sow cannot access (the creep). Enables piglets to begin adapting to solid food before weaning, reducing the post-weaning growth check.

content.text: The single most important factor in successful weaning is how well the piglets have been eating

before the sow's milk is removed. Piglets that are eating solid food confidently at weaning show a much smaller growth check than piglets weaned onto dry feed with no prior experience of it. Start offering creep from 10 to 14 days of age, even though very little will be consumed initially.
Remove the sow from the pen rather than moving the piglets. The piglets remain in their familiar space with familiar smells, reducing stress.
Keep the litter together for at least two more weeks before any further separation. Piglets benefit from the social warmth and familiarity of their litter-mates.
Offer the same creep feed used pre-weaning for the first two weeks. Abrupt changes to feed type at weaning cause digestive upset.
Ensure fresh water is always available. Newly weaned piglets drink significantly more than when nursing.
Reduce the sow's feed for the day before weaning to reduce milk let-down. Resume normal feeding from the day after weaning.
Check her udder on the day of weaning and daily for three days. Engorgement for 24 to 48 hours is normal. Hard, hot, painful glands or a temperature over 39.5°C suggests mastitis.
The sow should return to oestrus within 3 to 7 days of weaning. If you are planning a second litter, introduce the boar at this point.

A temporary reduction in growth rate for 5 to 10 days after weaning is normal. Piglets eating little, appearing quieter than usual, and producing loose droppings in the first three days does not always indicate disease. If symptoms persist beyond five days or if a piglet stops eating entirely, consult your vet.
